      Edit note

      Entering an edit note that describes where you got your information is highly recommended. Not only does it make it clear where you got your information, but it can also encourage other users to vote on your edit — thus making your edit get applied faster.

      Even just providing a URL or two is helpful! For more suggestions, see our guide for writing good edit notes.

      The name is the artist’s official name.

      Please see the style guidelines for more information.

      The sort name is an artist name variant used when sorting alphabetically.

      “Last Name, First Name” and “Group, The” are common examples of sort names.

      Please see the style guidelines for more information.

      The disambiguation field helps users distinguish between artists with identical or similar names. Feel free to leave it blank if it seems unlikely that there will be other artists with similar names.

      This field is not a place to store general background information. That kind of information should go in an annotation.

      Select any type from the list to see its description. If the entity doesn’t seem to match any type, just leave this blank. This indicates an individual person, be it under its legal name (“John Lennon”), or a performance name (“Sting”). A grouping of multiple musicians who perform together (in some cases, some or all of the members might differ in different performances or recordings). This indicates a choir/chorus (an organized, usually large group of singers). Smaller vocal ensembles and groupings that do not generally call themselves choirs are better entered as “Group”. This indicates an orchestra (an organized, usually large group of instrumentalists). Smaller ensembles (such as trios and quartets) and groupings that do not generally call themselves orchestras are better entered as “Group”. This indicates an individual fictional character (whether a fictional person, animal or any other kind of character). No description available.

      The gender field describes the gender with which a person or character identifies.

      Please see the style guidelines for more information.

      The area indicates the country the artist is primarily identified with. If the artist is strongly associated with an area smaller than a country, select that instead.

      Please see the style guidelines for more information.

      IPI codes are assigned by CISAC to “interested parties” in musical rights management.

      If you don’t know the code for this entity, just leave the field blank.

      ISNI codes are an ISO standard used to uniquely identify persons and organizations.

      If you don’t know the code for this entity, just leave the field blank.

      The begin and end dates describe when the artist was born and died. The begin and end dates describe when the group was formed and dissolved. The begin date is the real-life date when the character concept was created. The end date should not be set. The begin and end dates describe when the artist started and stopped existing.

      Please see the style guidelines for more information.

      The begin and end areas describe where the artist was born and died. The begin and end areas describe where the group was formed and dissolved. The begin area is the real-life area where the character concept was created. The end area should not be set. The begin and end areas describe where the artist was when it started and stopped existing.

      Please see the style guidelines for more information.

      External links are URLs associated with the artist. These can include the artist’s official homepage and social networking pages, streaming services, and unofficial pages like Wikipedia entries, biographies, interviews, and fan sites.

      Please don’t add a Wikipedia page if a Wikidata item linking to the same article already exists.
